title: Why orchestrate
subtitle: You can run one food truck alone; a fleet needs a manager who never sleeps
mission: api-pedidos runs 3 replicas spread over a few servers. Three things will happen: a server dies at 3 am, traffic triples at noon and a new version ships at 3 pm. Compare handling it by hand (docker run on each server) with an orchestrator like Kubernetes (with an autoscaler set up for the peak). Count how long the service stays below what was asked and how many people have to drop everything.

predict.question: with an orchestrator and 3 servers, at 3 am server-1 dies. What happens to the replica that was on it?

options.rescheduled: The orchestrator creates another one on a remaining server
options.waits: It stays down until someone wakes up and restarts it
options.gone: It’s gone for good: now there are only 2

feedback.right: right! You asked for 3 replicas, so the orchestrator works to keep 3. When the node disappears, it waits out the default toleration (about 5 minutes in Kubernetes), evicts its pods and recreates the replicas on the remaining servers. Nobody woke up.
feedback.wrong: look at the cluster: the pod on server-1 went Terminating and a new one showed up Running on another server, with nobody typing anything. You declare "I want 3"; the orchestrator fixes the difference.
feedback.skipped: no guess? Run it and look in the cluster for the new pod that showed up by itself.

coach.ui: guess noted. Run with orchestrator, then switch to manual. Compare "people woken up".
coach.cmd: guess noted. Run operate and then operate --way manual. Compare "people woken up".

tryNext.ui: Now leave a single server: not even an orchestrator works miracles with nowhere to send the replicas. Then try the "release" event.
tryNext.cmd: Run operate --servers 1 (not even an orchestrator works miracles without another server) and then operate --event release.

why.simples:
With one food truck, you handle it yourself: open, cook, close. With twenty trucks spread around town, someone has to coordinate: when one breaks down at 3 am, send another; at lunchtime, put more trucks on the street; change the menu without closing them all at once.
The orchestrator is that manager who never sleeps. You don’t say “start truck 3”; you say “I always want 3 trucks serving”, and she works to keep that true.
why.dev:
docker run handles one machine. With several, questions appear that it doesn’t answer: which server does each container run on? Who recreates what died? How do you change versions without taking the service down? How do containers find each other on the network?
Kubernetes answers with desired state: you declare it (a Deployment with replicas: 3) and controllers compare desired with actual all the time, fixing the difference. A pod that dies is recreated; a node that goes down has its pods recreated on other nodes (by default, after about 5 minutes of toleration); updates are gradual (a rolling update, which by default starts new pods before removing all the old ones) and you can go back with a rollback. Scaling with load needs setting up, for example, a HorizontalPodAutoscaler: it isn’t on by default.
why.especialista:
Orchestration has a cost: a control plane to maintain (or pay for, as on AKS, EKS and GKE), networking, storage, version upgrades a few times a year, RBAC, policies and observability. For a small app, a container PaaS (Azure Container Apps, Cloud Run) or one server with docker compose can be cheaper and simpler.
The default timings shape the design: a node with no news turns NotReady after a grace period, and its pods are only evicted when the 300 s tolerationSeconds Kubernetes adds by default runs out. To react faster, tune tolerations per pod; to not depend on it, spread replicas across nodes and zones (topologySpreadConstraints) and protect them during maintenance (PodDisruptionBudget). And self-healing isn’t high availability: with a single replica, every restart is an outage.

steps:
Install kind (kind.sigs.k8s.io) and kubectl (kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools). They use the Docker you already have. Create the file kind.yaml:
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
- role: control-plane
- role: worker
- role: worker

Create a cluster with 1 control-plane node and 2 workers. Each node is a container, as docker ps shows:
kind create cluster --name escola --config kind.yaml
docker ps

Load lesson 3’s image into the cluster and ask for 3 replicas (skipped lesson 3? use --image=nginx:alpine and skip kind load):
kind load docker-image api-pedidos:1.0 --name escola
kubectl create deployment api --image=api-pedidos:1.0 --replicas=3
kubectl get pods -o wide

Delete a pod and watch another take its place:
kubectl delete pod NAME-OF-A-POD
kubectl get pods

Now take down a whole node (it’s just a container) and watch for about 6 minutes; Ctrl+C exits -w:
docker stop escola-worker
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -o wide -w
When done: docker start escola-worker
recipe.ok: the deleted pod is replaced within seconds; with escola-worker stopped, it shows as NotReady and, after about 5 minutes (the default toleration), the replicas that were on it are recreated on the remaining node, and you’re back to 3 Running (the old ones may stay Terminating until the node returns).
